topics.title: Words 4: family and people
topics.intro: Sixteen people words. Several are third declension: the genitive (μητρός, ἀνδρός, παιδός) shows the stem. Learn each noun with its article and genitive, the way a dictionary gives it.
topics.teach: Teach the words for mother, father, son and daughter, with their genitives.
topics.talk: Ask {him} the Greek for “child” and which English word for a doctor comes from it.
topics.hook: Learn people words with their genitive: **μήτηρ, μητρός** → metropolis, a mother city.

topics.title: Words 5: the city and war
topics.intro: The words of Athens at war and at peace: city, people, army, ships, walls, council. Democracy is hiding in here.
topics.teach: Explain which two Greek words make “democracy”, and what each means.

topics.title: Words 6: sea, sky and land
topics.intro: Odysseus’ world: sea, wind, stars, mountains, islands and storms, plus two verbs for a sea voyage.
topics.teach: Explain why ἀφικνέομαι looks passive but is not.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which gas is named after the Greek for water.
topics.hook: **ὕδωρ** → hydrogen; **γῆ** → geography; **ἀστήρ** → asterisk, a little star.

topics.title: Words 7: gods, temples and heroes
topics.intro: Religion ran through Greek life: temples, priests, altars, sacrifices and oracles. And the heroes, half-way between gods and mortals.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between θάνατος and ἀθάνατος.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what the Oracle at Delphi was, and the Greek word for an oracle.
topics.hook: ἀ- (not) + **θάνατος** (death) = ἀθάνατος: the gods are the deathless ones.

topics.title: Words 8: home, food and animals
topics.intro: Everyday life: doors and tables, bread and wine, cows, sheep and dogs, and the verbs for eating, drinking and sleeping.
topics.teach: Explain how the Greek for “dog” gave us the word “cynical”.
topics.talk: At dinner, ask {him} the Greek for wine, bread and drink.

topics.title: Words 9: body, mind and feelings
topics.intro: Body parts (doctors still use them), and the feelings that drive every myth: fear, anger, hope and love.
topics.teach: Pick three medical words and explain the Greek inside each.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what an ophthalmologist and a cardiologist look after.

topics.title: Words 10: verbs of action
topics.intro: Sixteen verbs that do the work in every story. Many have a strong aorist with a different stem (λαμβάνω → ἔλαβον): learn the two together.
topics.teach: Teach four verbs with their aorists.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what “eureka” means and who said it.
topics.hook: Learn each verb with its aorist, like English go, went: **λαμβάνω, ἔλαβον**.

topics.title: Words 11: more verbs
topics.intro: Coming and going, asking and answering, giving and receiving. Watch for the verbs ending -ομαι that are active in meaning.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between ἐρωτάω and ἀποκρίνομαι.
topics.talk: Ask {him} the Greek for “I give” and which English medical word comes from it.
topics.hook: **-ομαι** verbs can be active in meaning: ἔρχομαι, I come; βούλομαι, I want.

topics.title: Words 12: adjectives
topics.intro: Sixteen describing words: big and small, many and few, easy and heavy. μέγας and πολύς are a little irregular, but you will meet them everywhere.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which English instruments come from βαρύς and ταχύς.

topics.title: Words 13: pronouns and questions
topics.intro: The small words that hold sentences together: I, you, we, this, that, who, what, where, when, how and why. Note the question mark ; at the end.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between τίς; and τις.
topics.talk: Ask {him} questions in Greek: ποῦ; πότε; πῶς;
topics.hook: **π-** asks, **τ-** answers: πότε; when? τότε, then.

topics.title: Words 14: numbers
topics.intro: Count to ten, then first, second, third, a hundred and a thousand. You already know most of them from maths and sport.
topics.teach: Count to ten in Greek and give an English word for each number.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what the Greek numbers are inside “decathlon” and “heptathlon”.

topics.title: Words 15: time and adverbs
topics.intro: Words for when and how: now, already, always, immediately, again. They are short, they never change their endings, and they are in almost every sentence.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between τότε and ἔπειτα.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to say “now”, “always” and “immediately” in Greek.
topics.hook: Little words that never change their endings: **νῦν** (now), **ἀεί** (always), **εὐθύς** (at once).

topics.title: Words 16: more prepositions and joining words
topics.intro: Nine more prepositions (each with its cases) and the conjunctions that join clauses: since, that, if, as, both… and.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between οὐ and μή.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to find a Greek preposition hiding in “hypodermic”, “perimeter” and “synthesis”.

topics.title: Words 17: big ideas and third-declension nouns
topics.intro: Nature, glory, excellence, contest and judgement: the ideas Greeks argued about. Many are third declension, so learn the genitive with the word.
topics.teach: Explain what ἀρετή means and why it is hard to translate with one English word.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how “protagonist” and “antagonist” come from ἀγών.
topics.hook: Learn the genitive with the word: **ὄνομα, ὀνόματος** → onomatopoeia.

topics.title: Vocabulary review: words 1 to 10
topics.intro: Mixed practice from the first ten sets: odd ones out, word families and words that are easy to confuse.
topics.teach: Explain how λόγος, λέγω and “dialogue” are related.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to name five Greek words for people.
topics.hook: Sort words into families: λόγος, λέγω and dialogue all speak.

items.prompt: **μανθάνω** means “I learn”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: μανθάνω (I learn) → mathematics.
items.hook: μαθ-, the aorist stem, → math-.

items.prompt: **πάσχω** means “I suffer”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: πάσχω (I suffer) → sympathy.
items.hook: σύν + πάθος: feeling with someone.

items.prompt: **γίγνομαι** means “I become, am born”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: γίγνομαι (I become, am born) → genesis.
items.hook: γεν- is the root: γένεσις, a coming into being.

items.prompt: **δίδωμι** means “I give”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: δίδωμι (I give) → antidote.
items.hook: ἀντί + δο- (give): something given against poison.

items.prompt: **μέγας** means “big, great”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: μέγας (big, great) → megaphone.
items.hook: μέγας + φωνή: a big voice.

items.prompt: **ταχύς** means “fast”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: ταχύς (fast) → tachometer.
items.hook: ταχύς + μέτρον: a speed-measurer.

items.prompt: **ὀλίγος** means “few”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: ὀλίγος (few) → oligarchy.
items.hook: ὀλίγος + ἄρχω: rule by the few.

items.prompt: **πέντε** means “five”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: πέντε (five) → pentathlon.
items.hook: πέντε + ἆθλον (contest): five events.

items.prompt: **χίλιοι** means “a thousand”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: χίλιοι (a thousand) → kilometre.
items.hook: χίλιοι → kilo- (by way of French): a thousand.

items.prompt: **ἑκατόν** means “a hundred”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: ἑκατόν (a hundred) → hectare.
items.hook: ἑκατόν, with its rough breathing → hect-: 100.

items.prompt: **περί** means “around”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: περί (around) → perimeter.
items.hook: περί + μέτρον: the measure around.

items.prompt: **ὑπέρ** means “over, beyond”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: ὑπέρ (over, beyond) → hyperbole.
items.hook: ὑπέρ + βάλλω: throwing beyond.

items.prompt: **ὁ ἀγών** means “contest, struggle”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: ὁ ἀγών (contest, struggle) → antagonist.
items.hook: ἀντί + ἀγών: the one who struggles against you.

items.prompt: **ἡ φύσις** means “nature”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: ἡ φύσις (nature) → physics.
items.hook: φ = ph, υ = y: φύσις → phys-.

items.prompt: **ὁ χρυσός** means “gold”. Which English word comes from it?
items.explain: ὁ χρυσός (gold) → chrysanthemum.
items.hook: χρυσός + ἄνθεμον (flower): the golden flower.

items.prompt: Why do Greek dictionaries give a noun’s genitive, as in ἡ μήτηρ, τῆς μητρός?

options.text: The genitive shows the stem you add the other endings to
Because the genitive is the most common case
options.feedback: It is given because it shows the stem (μητρ-), which the nominative can hide.

options.text: To show the noun is feminine
options.feedback: The article (ἡ) shows the gender; the genitive shows the stem.

items.explain: μήτηρ hides the stem μητρ-; the genitive μητρός shows it.
items.hook: Learn nouns as a dictionary gives them: article, nominative, genitive: ἡ μήτηρ, τῆς μητρός.

items.prompt: What does **οἱ παῖδες** mean?

options.feedback: οἱ is plural, and so is the ending -ες.

items.explain: παῖς, παιδός: plural παῖδες, “children”.
items.hook: Third-declension plural subjects end -ες: παῖδες, πατέρες.

items.prompt: ἡ ναῦς (ship) is irregular. Which form means “the ships” (subject)?
items.explain: ναῦς, νεώς, νηΐ, ναῦν; plural νῆες. Easy to confuse with ναός (temple) and ναύτης (sailor).
items.hook: Three look-alikes: ναῦς ship, ναός temple, ναύτης sailor.

items.prompt: What is the genitive of **ἡ πόλις**?

options.feedback: πόλις has an unusual genitive: πόλεως.
πόλις is feminine and third declension.

items.explain: πόλις, πόλεως: an unusual genitive, with the accent still on the first syllable.
items.hook: πόλις, πόλεως: the odd genitive keeps its accent at the front.

items.prompt: Why does ἀθάνατος have only two sets of endings (ἀθάνατος, ἀθάνατον), not three?

options.text: Compound adjectives like this use the masculine form for the feminine too
It is a noun, not an adjective
options.feedback: It is an adjective: αἱ ἀθάνατοι θεαί, the immortal goddesses.
They do: it is about how the adjective is built (ἀ- + θάνατος).

items.explain: ἀ- (not) + θάνατος (death): compound adjectives usually have two endings, so ἡ ἀθάνατος θεά.
items.hook: Compounds with ἀ- use one form for masculine and feminine: ἡ ἀθάνατος θεά.

items.prompt: Which is the aorist of λαμβάνω (I take)?

options.feedback: That is the imperfect: “I was taking”.
That is the future: “I will take”.

items.explain: Strong aorist: a short stem λαβ- with the augment: ἔλαβον.
items.hook: Strong aorist = shorter stem: λαμβάνω → ἔλαβον.

items.prompt: Which case follows βοηθέω (I help) and μάχομαι (I fight)?

options.feedback: Most verbs take the accusative, but these two take the dative.
ἄρχω (I rule) takes the genitive; these take the dative.

items.explain: βοηθῶ τοῖς φίλοις, “I help my friends”; μάχονται τοῖς πολεμίοις, “they fight the enemy”.
items.hook: Help and fight take the dative: give help **to** someone, fight **with** someone.

items.prompt: ἀποκρίνομαι, δέχομαι, βούλομαι and γίγνομαι all end -ομαι. What does that ending show in these verbs?

options.text: They are deponent: middle endings with an active meaning
They are always in the future
options.feedback: They are present tense: “I answer”, “I receive”.

items.explain: Deponent verbs have middle endings (-ομαι, -ῃ, -εται…) but active meanings.
items.hook: A deponent is dressed as a middle but acts active.

items.prompt: Which phrase means “the great city”?

options.feedback: πόλις is feminine, so the article and adjective must be feminine.

items.explain: πόλις is feminine: ἡ μεγάλη πόλις.
items.hook: μέγας, μεγάλη, μέγα: only the feminine has the -αλ- stem here.

items.prompt: What does **αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς** mean?

options.feedback: The same king is ὁ αὐτὸς βασιλεύς, with αὐτός after the article.
Outside the article phrase, αὐτός means “self”.

items.explain: Position matters: αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς = the king himself; ὁ αὐτὸς βασιλεύς = the same king.
items.hook: Outside the article = self: αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς. Straight after the article = same: ὁ αὐτὸς βασιλεύς.

items.prompt: τίς (with an accent, in a question) means “who?”. What does τις (no accent, after a word) mean?

options.feedback: Without the accent it is the indefinite: “someone”.

items.explain: τίς ἐστιν; = who is it? ἄνθρωπός τις = a certain man, someone.
items.hook: Accent = a question: τίς; who? No accent = someone.

items.prompt: Which form of “one” goes with ἡ ναῦς (a feminine noun)?
items.explain: εἷς, μία, ἕν: μία ναῦς, one ship.
items.hook: εἷς, μία, ἕν: masculine, feminine and neuter “one”.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses μή correctly?

options.text: ὁ δοῦλος μὴ φεύγει. (The slave does not run away.)
options.feedback: A plain statement of fact uses οὐ: ὁ δοῦλος οὐ φεύγει.

options.text: μή ἐστι σοφός. (He is not wise.)
options.feedback: A statement of fact uses οὐ: οὐκ ἔστι σοφός.

items.explain: οὐ denies facts; μή is for commands, wishes, “if” clauses and purposes.
items.hook: οὐ for facts, μή for orders.

items.prompt: Why is it **symphony** but **synthesis**?

options.text: σύν becomes συμ- before φ, π, β and μ
They come from different Greek words

options.feedback: It is Greek: σύν + φωνή, “sounding together”.

items.explain: σύν + φωνή → συμφωνία; σύν + τίθημι → σύνθεσις.
items.hook: συν- becomes συμ- before π, φ, β, μ because it is easier to say.

items.prompt: Why is ἀρετή hard to translate with one English word?

options.text: It means being excellent at what you are for: courage in a soldier, skill in a craftsman, goodness in a person
It has no meaning on its own
options.feedback: It has a rich meaning: excellence of every kind.

options.text: It is a name, not a word
options.feedback: It is an ordinary noun (though Ἀρετή was also imagined as a goddess).

items.explain: ἀρετή: excellence, courage, virtue. Homer’s heroes fight to show their ἀρετή.
items.hook: ἀρετή = being the best at what you are for.

items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?

options.feedback: μήτηρ is a family member, like the others.

items.explain: mother, father, daughter… and a horse.
items.hook: Sort by meaning: three family words, and a horse.

items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?

options.feedback: πόλεμος (war) belongs with battle and weapon.
μάχη (battle) belongs with war and weapon.
ὅπλον (weapon) belongs with war and battle.

items.explain: war, battle, weapon… and peace.
items.hook: War, battle, weapon… and εἰρήνη, peace, as in the name Irene.

items.prompt: λόγος (word), λέγω (I say) and διάλογος (dialogue) share a root. What does the root mean?
items.explain: λεγ-/λογ-: say, speak, word. Logic, dialogue, lexicon.
items.hook: λεγ- and λογ- = speak: logic, dialogue, lexicon.

items.prompt: Which pair belongs to the same family?

options.feedback: They only look alike: πόλις is city, πολύς is many.
Look-alikes: ναός is a temple, ναῦς a ship.

items.explain: πόλεμος → πολέμιος, “of war, hostile”; οἱ πολέμιοι, “the enemy”.
items.hook: πόλεμος → πολέμιος: one family. πόλις and πολύς only look alike.

items.prompt: Which word means “temple”?
items.explain: ναός (temple), ναῦς (ship), ναύτης (sailor): three easy-to-confuse words.
items.hook: ναός (temple) has an ο; ναῦς (ship) has a υ.

items.prompt: Which word means “I see”?
items.explain: ὁράω (aorist εἶδον): panorama.
items.hook: ὁράω, I see → panorama, a view of everything.

items.prompt: εἶδον is the aorist of which verb?

options.feedback: A clever guess: they are related, but εἶδον is the aorist of ὁράω.

items.explain: εἶδον = I saw. Learn irregular aorists with their verbs.
items.hook: εἶδον, I saw → idea.

items.prompt: An “ophthalmic surgeon” is a doctor who…
items.explain: ὀφθαλμός = eye; χειρουργία (surgery) = hand-work.
items.hook: ὀφθαλμός (eye) + χειρουργία (hand-work): an eye surgeon.

items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?

options.feedback: ποῦ; is a question word, like the others.

items.explain: where? when? how?… and a door.
items.hook: π- question words: ποῦ; πότε; πῶς;

items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?
items.explain: five, seven, ten… and “quick”.
items.hook: Three numbers and an adjective: ταχύς, as in tachometer.

items.prompt: Which English word is built from πᾶς (all) + θεός (god)?

options.feedback: pandemic is πᾶς + δῆμος: affecting all the people.

items.explain: The Pantheon in Rome was a temple to all the gods.
items.hook: πᾶς + θεός: all the gods.
items.example: The Pantheon in Rome, whose name means a temple of all the gods, still stands today.

items.prompt: Which word means “wisdom”?
items.explain: σοφία: philosophy, Sophie.
items.hook: σοφία → Sophie and philosophy.

items.prompt: What does **ὑπὸ τοῦ στρατηγοῦ** mean in “the army was led by the general”?

options.feedback: With a person in the genitive after a passive verb, ὑπό means “by”.

items.explain: ὑπό + genitive of a person = “by”: the agent of a passive verb.
items.hook: ὑπό + genitive of a person + passive verb = by.

items.prompt: Which of these verbs is deponent (middle ending, active meaning)?
items.explain: ἀφικνέομαι, βούλομαι, γίγνομαι, δέχομαι, ἔρχομαι, μάχομαι: all -ομαι, all active in meaning.
items.hook: -ομαι with an active meaning = deponent.

items.prompt: The modern heptathlon has seven events. Which Greek number is inside it?
items.explain: ἑπτά (seven) + ἆθλον (prize, contest).
items.hook: ἑπτά (7) + ἆθλον (contest) = heptathlon.

items.prompt: Which Greek word best describes the excellence a hero strives to show?

options.feedback: κίνδυνος is danger: what a hero faces, not what he has.
ὀργή is anger: Achilles had plenty, but it is not excellence.

items.explain: ἀρετή: excellence of every kind, the quality every hero strives to show.
items.hook: Heroes chase ἀρετή; what they face is κίνδυνος.
